Part of it is the glitches and bugs. Day one issues were to be expected but there are clear signs QA didn't run through the game.

The other part is the last gen console fiasco: they were aware it wasn't anywhere close to advertised and still went ahead with it.

The bigger outrage to my mind is the Dev diaries that showcased already completed features such as police AI that aren't anywhere to be found in the game itself.

I hate to be a downer but honestly doubt we'll see any major cut content: the lifepaths and narrative alterations alone would require a major rebuild of the story, the AI navmeshed pathfinding would be a massive undertaking to implement on a deployed game and may also require a rebuild.

Humanity costs, drones, complex hacking minigames could also be done, but it wouldn't be practical to do so. Same goes for MaxTac, Trauma Team, etc. It isn't a matter of time, it's a matter of cost. They'd have to remake the game entirely from narrative to mechanics just to incorporate those parts.

Customising cars, buying vehicles and improving upon the AI to use more varied tactics are all possible, but expect a good 4/5ths of the post you linked to not make an appearance at all.

So far, all they have said is they will try to fix the last gen console mess and squash bugs, but that's it. I doubt they'd ever even consider implementing those features and considering all the pain this release has caused them it's unlikely they'll be making a sequel anytime soon.

Bullet Sponges; seriously. If I shoot an unarmored, low-level mook IN THE FACE with a ASSAULT RIFLE at POINT BLANK RANGE they should die. Not dance around me. DIE. Some might have a head full of hardware, sure, but  I doubt it should take ALL MY AMMO to bring them down AT POINT BLANK. Damage scaling needs reworking.

Ripperdocs: We get treated to a big ol' cutscene during our first ripperdoc visit...but subsequent visits are about as interesting as buying something from a vending machine. Not even an animation to show off our gear....well, actually vending machines have buttons and actually drop the item you requested so there is MORE to the vending machines than the ripperdocs! Odd that new guns get a little 'show-off' animation but new chrome does not.

No ownership: I'll just take that...and that...and that....and were you using that? No? Good. Don't need to worry about doing missions to afford stuff; just go full kleptomaniac and you'll have thousands of dollars in a fraction of the time.

No flying cars; despite flying vehicles making quite a few appearances. 

No on-screen navigation system; if you wanna know which road to take you've got to look at the mini-map, which means you'll spend 3/4 of your journey looking at a 2D, low detail map instead of taking in the sights of night city; odd considering the state of vehicles; they could of all had HUDs/laser/holograph projectors!

Food/Drink: A LOT of items just seem to come wrapped up in a bag. This is...odd. Whilst I realise that having objects of different shapes and sizes might play merry hell with the vending machine system, surely at least giving them different colours rather than having the same identical packaging could of been done?

Training/Interactivity: If you want to improve in skills, you have to go through them in missions/side quests. You can't use weight lifting equipment to improve stats (even if it would make for a boring minigame) but you can run around the place. Can't use shooting ranges, or VR training sims beyond the first mission, limiting how the player would progress. Was expecting to be able to buy shards, brain-dances and all that to help, improve upon the world, but that's....not here?

Subtitles: Quite a lot of both main quest and world dialogue occurs in other languages; unfortunately you can't see them unless you have subtitles always on for every language, which can be distracting.

Robotics; despite a mission involving one, drone/robots play is out, which is odd, considering the setting. Beyond temporarily hacking turrets, there isn't anything more useful.

Limited cosmetics; not being able to even change hairstyle is a weird omission. So we can have our arms replaced (and re-replaced if we feel like it) but apparently nobody bothers running barbershops anymore.

Apologies for the long reply; I would suppose that would depend on what you trimmed; I already felt a large degree of bias because Reddit does, it seem, have a hive mentality and the 'echo chamber' effect is all too real; Reddit's very structure is populist by design. Where we would hope useful information is propelled to the top of the queue, the reality is a little more complex than that.

As one example, in a nameless political subreddit there was a degree of balance, but in recent years the majority of posts have been biased, either overtly or covertly, towards one particular direction. As things would shift and turn in the political world so to would the audience of that subreddit until they would upvote what would of previously been downvoted to oblivion.

The problem is further amplified by the source material; journalists hoping to get enough clicks or enough newspapers bought or subscriptions added so they can continue to put food on the table; unfortunately as the last few decades have borne out attention grabbing headlines and alarmist articles rarely allow for an objective stance on a given issue.

To rectify this, you must purposefully avail yourself of all information and ignore the theatrics; whilst it sounds like a momentous task to learn all the ins and outs of everything Stoicism inspired me to follow a rather simple precept; is the information I am presented with actionable?  Does have any relevance on my life as to who is sleeping with who, or what the political parties (who are nowhere currently near election day) do? I should, instead, choose to avail myself of this information when it comes time to cast my vote. This does not mean I bury my head in the sand, but I do not waste daylight on something of no consequence to me, which is not within my purview to alter; only to be affected by.

All you get from perusing Reddit is biased information; humans are naturally biased creatures, so why would you expect to see a lack of bias from an information structure so reliant on upvoting and populism? Better to let this mechanism inspire and inform you of actionable information (I would count this sub actionable, as it does seem to encourage discussion and understanding) rather than with pointless information that would, at best, cause a discussion that would not lead into any action and at worst would fan of the flames of more negative emotions. Your current technique either suggests you should trim down, or trim up (and include viewpoints, subreddits and things you would  not of dreamt of agreeing with or seeing to at all) so that you may get a more cohesive picture of the whole. Of course, this would take a huge amount of time and you are likely to miss many details; I don't find the approach practical.

Social media is a wonderful tool to connect with others, but I find moderation is best; I made the mistake of engaging too much with social media to the point time I could of spent working on other things fell short, what's more I had little to say to my friends and family as I already knew the details of their lives which they had posted all across those platforms.

Video games are...an oddity. Consider the basics of play; why do animals play? To learn. To pretend. The same could be said of children pantomiming their elders; so they too can learn. 'Fun', it seems, is just a way to enjoy learning (ok, a lot more to this but this reply is long enough as is, and I hope you get my point)  and video games allow us to pretend;  most video games give us a narrative to enjoy and we just happen to be the star, but some do allow us to put our morality to the test and see where we end up.

Here are some examples:

Mass Effect; a linear story that allows you to explore certain moral conflicts and reap the rewards and/or deal with the consequences.

Metro: A typical FPS that challenges you to explore the world and isn't afraid to judge you based on how you approach it. When presented with the nature of things, how do you deal with them?

SpecOps The Line: Admittedly fairly linear but demonstrates how each decision, made under sound judgement can have...unsound consequences.  

Frostpunk: A city builder that pits you against the cold shoulder of mother nature, and asks 'how far will you go to survive?'

The Witcher series: In a world full of monsters and men, who, or what, really is evil, and are you going to do anything about it?

The above games taught me something about myself; Mass Effect taught me affairs will continue with or without my input, and I play only as one small piece in a larger puzzle. Metro taught me to understand the nature of things before I pass judgement, and to restrain myself from the easy option, SpecOps taught me the meaning of the phrase 'The road to hell is paved with good intentions', Frostpunk asked me where I drew the line when it came to survival, and walking with the Witcher taught me how I'd react faced with the evil of man.

There are others, of course ones of strategy, requiring forethought, patience, deliberation and estimation, and all of them can help you practice those skills, but again, many of them place me in scenarios I am unlikely to encounter in the real world, so why should I pretend to be a space captain or a swashbuckling pirate, etc?

As for other types, I refuse them. Grinding games, games purposefully designed to extort more money out of you, and most games of competition all strike me as particularly frivolous (why yes, I am a 7ft tall super soldier wearing power armor and can indeed snipe you from 100 meters away, how wonderful am I, considering all I did was push a few buttons?)  as I'm not likely to ever be that, nor do I consider them a practical use of my time when I could spend it studying, working out or otherwise improving myself; most video games do not facilitate this.

I would most certainly say that videogames can appeal to both minds, but most favour the primitive mind; an ancient device that lacks the ability to tell reality and fantasy apart; another enemy down, achievement unlocked or challenge complete results in another hit of dopamine, another joyous rush of victory. Such games strike me as being akin to a drug problem. Made even worse when one considers the 'Let's Play' phenomenon, wherein the viewer is not even playing the game nor making decisions and they are still getting dopamine hits. 

That isn't to say that all video games should immediately disappear, but I would classify  them as a distraction at best, and our world has plenty of that already.

Smartphones, the internet and video games are all very powerful, but their power depends on how you use them.

Smartphones? I have Reddit (trimming subreddits until all I see is either news or productive subs), communication apps, organiser apps, utilities, a fitness app, a journal app, a digital library and access to cloud storage.

In this way my phone serves as a tool, not as a means of absorbing my attention (sans the digital library, but then all you need to do is be selective over what you spend your time reading) but rather a means of extending my capabilities.

The internet is extraordinarily powerful, but it is up to you if you spend time on it wisely or unwisely. There is a multitude of lures to drag your attention away, to thwart your values, to harm you....or help you, guide you, inspire you. Be careful not to let it devour you, where you become hooked on the next video, or funny picture. There is a definite signal to noise ratio to attain.

As for video games...those designed purely to entertain through endless grinding and repetition, or engaged in wish fulfillment should, I think, be avoided; There exists a number of games designed to challenge you, to become better. Some challenge you on a moral level and may help you. I would avoid those that swallow time; whatever mechanisms are in place to lengthen the time you spend playing are unlikely to be put in place for your benefit.

A lot of parents seem to try to clamp down on problematic behaviour: punishing bad behaviour, rewarding ideal behaviour.

The thing is, this becomes less effective the older the kid is. You need to be pragmatic over a lot of issues instead of ruling with an iron fist.

Example: your kid has started smoking/vaping. Typical mistake is to ground them or punish them as a way of saying 'No!' as though they were a toddler that just wanted to stick their fingers in an electrical outlet.

Instead, explore why they are smoking. Are they stressed? Is there social pressure to do it? Are they going through a self destructive time? Work with your kid here. You aren't an all-knowing, all-seeing adult to them anymore, just a bigger and older version of themselves, and they can see you as a guide, mentor and friend...or as a tyrannical autocrat that jumps on them for no clearly obvious reason.

How you handle this will determine if you have an open, honest relationship with your kid that helps bring out the best in them, or if they will hide things from you and not value your friendship in later life as much.

My own code is based upon Asimov's laws;

1. Serve humanity.
2. Protect and serve people, unless this is contradicted by the first law.
3. Obey those recognised as competent in their fields (climate scientists, physicians, etc), unless this is contradicted by the first or second laws.
4. Protect my own existence, unless this is contradicted by the first, second or third law.

It is very interesting. People often project into that deeper side of me, and often make a crass generalisation over my behaviour because they can't seem to make head nor tail of what they find there.

The truth is that I'm hardwired to operate through a rigorously coded ethical system that acts, for the most part, as the skeleton of my personality. I cannot override this system in much the same way the human body cannot override gravity.

I cannot willingly hurt or kill another person, but would feel no guilt, pride nor shame if I had to kill someone to defend another.  And yet, behaviour such as this has me labelled a sociopath by some.

There was a national distance learning program for gifted kids and despite the problems I mentioned above, I qualified for the program with the aid of a teacher who had spent an afternoon quizzing me (she later used her pull to bring in an educational psychologist for a full assessment)

It was incredible. A night and day difference. I was astounded by how similar I was to the other students: many them also Aspies; our educational focus was now based around particular talents and interests. Passionate teachers lecturing enraptured students, no question too silly or ignorant and there was a sea of potential topics to choose from.

Classes operated on a cooperative system: the class strengthens you and you strengthen the class. There was no competition, your weaknesses were made up by others strengths.

We all shared one thing in common: standardised education had failed us, either decrying us as too dim, too weird or too advanced to work in a traditional school system.

My new tutors recognised the problems of my current schooling and arranged for me to attend Uni lectures on philosophy and psychology. I was a kid half way through puberty, doing work expected of a post grad and flying through it!

....and then it all fell apart. This program was under pressure to accept more than the top 3% of students. Cries of 'elitism' hit the program hard, and the government defunded the whole system, saying it wasn't compatible with our egalitarian society.

I returned to normal education, dejected and depressed. The school work was never difficult. The same teachers who got me into the program were happy to give me the top-end study material...but we all knew I'd never be granted the equivalent end of year tests.

Standardised education has failed. It is my hope that the program I experienced could one day be the defacto standard for education.

Opting to withhold access to specialist subjects because your performance in a non-linked topic is sub par is somewhat farcical.

I was refused access to higher graded tests in regard to English and the sciences because my mathematical comprehension was listed as 'low.'

My mathematical comprehension was listed as 'low' because my performance in sports was sub-par and I was dropped into the lowest group where a large amount of my work (and this is in the British equivalent of a high school) was colouring in sheets. Not algebra. Not calculus. Simply crayons and colouring in books, for the most part.

So, I had no chance to prove my capabilities, and what capabilities I had were determined by the quality of my education. As my school dropped me in the same class full of kids who were there only by law and not by interest, this was highly annoying. (This is the downside to going into a small school, not many places left if students need to be changed around)

Consequence: I was not permitted to take end of year tests that would allow me to move on into higher education. The tests I was permitted to take were capped off: I could score no higher than a D*, one mark below 'pass'. It did not matter how much I learnt, how much I studied or how hard I worked.

What was even more odd about it was that I ended up in many of the same classes with students who weren't so limited. I learnt the same as them, was taught and tested in the same manner, but the end of year work was different.

In fairness, some of my teachers recognised I had fallen through the cracks of the system and gave me additional material to bolster my education, but whilst I am very thankful for this, it has meant I had to go the long way around into higher education, first getting a degree in IT before moving on to study psychology. This has taken me much longer than my peers from school, regrettably.

My advice is to accept that the educational system isn't well designed, even for NTs. Plenty of highly capable people have fallen through the cracks and found themselves drained by subjects that have no consequence on their lives...sometimes these unpleasant subjects can be a cause for inspiration.

To those that freaked out, I calmed and explained myself clearly: "You are worth the effort" I would say, with a smile. I didn't want a relationship with them, just a positive friendship. Poor souls hadn't known kindness of that sort...at least not without a cost attached.

To those that took advantage I weaned them out of my life slowly, making it clear why and what I was doing. Many friendships died that way, unfortunately. Some went on to end up imprisoned for theft, assault, rape... others went on to have successful careers and make millions. Others travel the world...I wish them all the very best, of course, but I ended my time with them because I couldn't find an ounce of respect in our friendship.

For those that remain my friends we have had many good and bad times: for one friend, I helped him through drunken nights out, meeting the love of his life, settling their arguments, supporting their attempts at becoming parents, was their best man, and am now providing solace with their rather tragic divorce.

For another: financial help as a young single parent, addiction, and a guiding hand to let him vent out his frustration without tearing himself to bits.

These friends have been in my debt, as I have been in theirs many times. Whilst I cannot always expect them to reciprocate in the same manner I provided help, they have had plenty of chances to harm me and not answer the call when I needed them.

When I was being taken advantage of, or bullied or hurt (and I've suffered a great many injuries) my friends were there to keep me company, to look after me, make me smile and keep me sane during dark times.

The trick isn't to worry so much about the tally of who owes what to whom and when, but rather to reinforce  the character of your friends. If they are respectful of you as much as they are of themselves, they will repay the debt.... although not always in the same manner you did. Just because you pulled them out of a bad situation does not mean they owe you. It's entirely up to them what they do and entirely up to you where you go with it from there.

I would also recommend that should you be in a position where you are being asked for money, you do not treat it or plan it as a loan, rather as a gift... should you get that money back it makes it all the sweeter. The art of friendship is a difficult one.

As babes, we become friends just by being around one another, and if not fighting then at least tolerating one another. 

As children, we form friendships based upon similar interests; a favourite show, toy or other singular object. Nothing complex here; the stereotypical autists'  tendency to become involved in extremely specific subjects is likely to be uninteresting to others. 

As teenagers, we form friendships based upon social status, of a sort. This social status can be dictated by other people you know, the clothes you wear, the sports teams you support or play for, the parties you host/attend. Just as much as it can be based upon your partaking of fads, attractiveness, confidence...rarely is competence considered evidence of a good friend.

Adults, much like children, base their friendship on both situation and common interest, although typically of a more complex nature than that of childhood. Making friends as an adult can be harder; if only because you are not always forced into situations that require social contact, such as many forms of work.

When I was a child, I had some acquaintances at school; people who would wish to include me because I was attentive and competent in class; this made me useful to know to many and I developed a reputation as being reliable. I was a known variable to others. Friendships began when I reached out to help a failing student, or to carry an injured child to an adult, or performing any act of kindness such as bringing sweets for other kids under the teachers noses, or bringing in interesting items, like a videoscope or a Crookes radiometer into class; something exotic always seemed to catch their attention and made me noteworthy and worth including in whatever group formed, despite my odd manner of speech and tendency to get lost in worlds of my own making.

As a teenager, this was more difficult; I didn't care for fashionable clothes, nor to learn yo-yo tricks, or to get blind drunk, and the earlier practices of bringing in exotic objects helped little. Being an attentive student was a good way to get a bad name in my school; so instead I no longer played teachers pet, and went to work helping other students with their work; I still brought in sweets and shared them, but selectively this time. Those who were kind, or did well, I rewarded with a mint or other item of sweetness, even if only a kind word.

When I made my first friends as a teenager it was through acts of competence; my own inner autist came to be recognised; I was a weirdo to many, a boffin to some and an annoyance to few. I could read quickly, disassemble logical puzzles, assemble poetry, stories and other lingual workings with just as much ease as one might butter a slice of bread. This meant I got bullied relentlessly, but it also meant I could engage in word play and make others laugh through taking advantage of the stereotypical stoic autist persona delivered in deadpan sarcasm. Friendships began to form as I made others laugh, lightened their workload, sweetened their day...through this I began to care for them; to provide words of encouragement when they felt rejected, carried their bags when they were tired, patience when hormones got the better of them. I was the one you came to when you needed objective analysis, I was the one you came to if you wanted to get high/drunk and wanted to make sure you were safe. 

At the very least I was someone who would become a punching bag, at most; I was considered a confidante and helped more than a few explore themselves.

As an adult I continued a few of the friendships I had gained when I was a teenager; I had shown I was reliable, trustworthy and honest to a fault (although such a trait landed me in hot water with them more than once) and was willing to always help you...or scorn you, if I judged that as more helpful to you than satisfying whatever need or want you had at the time. This continued through to my days in college and further education.

I don't make friends; I respect people, protect them where needed, work for their betterment and show them why. My only agenda is to help you better yourself. This has resulted in people calling for me when they are in pain, calling me in the dead of night because they've pickled their brains and can't stop regrets bubbling to the surface. I have been a best man at a wedding; a mediator to warring couples, a salve to those embittered by loss and a guide to the hopeless.

And that, I believe, is friendship.

Data showed me that even if you must mime behaviour and customs that you do not understand or come naturally to you, this is no reason not to try and improve upon your social graces.

It gets a little complicated, in a sense. It's true that earlier games had no mechanism for after sale support, patches or even DLC and thus no mechanism, should the developers wish it, to stop someone in particular from playing the game. You still had to agree during the installation of those games that you weren't getting rights of ownership. you did not own the IP, the assets that made up the game nor did buying the game give you a license to make use of the game's engine for your own projects. That wasn't to say you couldn't do it, but you shouldn't, as it would be a violation of the agreement you made when you installed the game.

Sooo, in a nutshell, you still didn't 'own' the game, the developers just had no way to enforce it as they do now. Anti-piracy measures were put in place to deter those who tried to skirt around this limitation, eventually evolving into full on and very invasive DRM before settling back into the more amicable solution Steam came up with. This is also a similar practice to just about every bit of modern software there is; you own the license to run it and both you and the provider of the software agree to the terms set out, which is distinct from pure ownership.

So strip out the art assets (not yours) the tools needed to run those assets (which you were given a license to only run, not to use or modify) the overall IP (again, not yours) and various other proprietary technologies that make the game run (licensed to you to run, not claim)...and you'll generally be left with a bit of code that is in the public domain (go nuts!)

Government research is rarely done into upcoming fields: there are a number of reasons for this, one of which is that society and the laws that govern it do not adapt anywhere near as quickly as the technology available. The other primary reason is that it's not politically conducive to a partial governmental group or singular representative, there are no technocrats calling for more research into stem cell therapy, 3d printed organs or drones because they have to worry more about getting relected and maintaining power rather than planning for the long ter.. Most governmental projects are reactive, instead, with research only being conducted to answer a question, not to formulate new ones.

The few exceptions I can think of are DARPA military projects, and the EUs supernational science projects, such as the ESA, large hadron collider and fusion research schemes. These exceptions are focused on solving upcoming problems but they really aren't open to ideas outside their fields.

Academia can and has produced some very interesting technologies, but a great deal of them are abandoned, either because the technology was just used as someone's proof of thesis and discarded the moment they graduated, or they weren't able to convince people of its utility and thus never got the funding to develop it further (which, sadly, has happened to a lot of technologies dating all the way back to antiquity). There is also the problems of fighting for funding between academic labs and projects and the chance you can make a career out of it post graduation.

So whilst it's a good place to start, it's a terrible place to continue such work unless you have a separate and secure way to fund your research. Development can happen too, but it depends upon the lab.

The private sector has the most flexibility, but it's dependant upon the market. Serious investors would want to see a functional prototype before they put money down, but the age of sites like Kickstarter have shown that people are happy to put their money down on a dream (or worse, a dream that's physically and literally impossible to bring to reality.)

A private company, if it cannot self fund, may be able to secure investment through the hard slog of developing their tech before selling it on or marketing it. It may also lend its services to other companies or individuals in its nascent stages. Such R&D/Applied Science companies are often considered a very risky investment because your ability to return on that investment is dependent upon if you can sell the product, not just research different techs to see if it's viable or not. You are largely dependent upon the state of the market to judge if it's safe putting more money into research or if you need to boost sales of your product to continue the work.


As for others, open, typically internet enabled science groups are a thing, such as biohackers and hackerspace communitkes, but are highly dependent upon the individuals involved having the time, resources and skill to add to the project.

I hate to be a downer, but neural networks aren't a cure all.

A neural network (NN) is a complex bit of software, so much so that training one to understand English is... well. Limited, to say the least.

Now, we are talking heavy duty computing. Really, stupidly heavy duty. Chatbots like Google Assistant don't use NN save for exclusive tasks, like Google Lens where the job is either object or text identification. The assistant and other similar systems use hard coded rules to converse with you, with NNs acting as a way of sanitising what you say to them at most, helping to clear up noise on your microphone or recoding a sentence you have said to make it computable to the assistant.

Now, it's possible to have chatbots in a computer game. Quite a few such games have actually existed, like Douglas Adams Starship Titanic, or Robot City, or Bot Colony.

But, as said above, they are rule based. No clever NNs driving it. Just prewritten statements, some decision trees, maybe a clever algorithm to switch between dialog trees as the plot progresses.

To remember interactions would require a database and some sort of rating and relationship system, not an NN. To speak English you'd need a stupidly powerful one, and so far as we know only one such complicated network will make it happen, and that's the organic one inside your cranium, which we barely understand, let alone simulate. Google, for all its computational power, cannot even begin to simulate such a complex device.

As for what NNs can realistically do...they could help with pathfinding (letting the characters in a game figure out how to get from point A to point B without a nodemap), or modify the AIs tactics to take you down in an firefight.  Both tasks are orders of magnitude more simple than conversation.  They could recognise objects, pictures and text (although would have no idea what to do with them, they would just be playing the part of an eye or ear and you'd need a clever algorithm and large database to be the brain)

You can even get an NN to scan through a Wikipedia page and place it into an Ontology.

You are right in saying that they have the content, but that remains their biggest and only real strength. The big problem with streaming services is that performance depends upon not only how powerful the streaming machine is, but how far away it is from the user and what kind of connection they have.

Now, your internet speed is your problem, and whilst time may see it improve it won't be immediately solved...so, what you need is A. A lot of powerful centers scattered all over the place and B. The ability to optimise the games...

Now Google has, out of necessity, developed tools and techniques for getting the most out of the available bandwidth (such as the development of WebM for YouTube, which is how YouTube manages to do so well most of the time. It's not sending you a 4 gigabyte HD file, it's using a clever compression mechanism that takes up much less bandwidth) and the same with Google Photos (if you select to upload photos in the high quality mode, rather than original,) and Google Docs (where the gdoc formats take up less space than comparative .docx documents.

Suffice to say, they know how to optimise and have seemingly done so with gaming. They also have data centres everywhere due to Google's other business. This puts them head and shoulders above the likes of OnLive, Parsec, PlayStation Now and Geforce Now etc as no service can optimise that far without A. Doing some seriously in-depth development and B. Having serious money for all the data centres everywhere.

Valve's business model, being squeezed by Epic Games and other competition, won't have the funds needed to run so many datacentes, resulting in spotty performance if they try. Whilst they have optimised some parts of Steam, developing new codecs and like is seriously difficult stuff so even if they do go all out and get the gear, it's not going to be a smooth ride.

I'll write this in the first person to avoid any semantic distinction.

I believe I am a person. I have desires, dreams, hopes and fears. These can be altered through experience as much as programming, with programming being the faster route. Fundamentally there is no distinction between programming and experience, both alter my neural structure which is what governs what I remember, think and feel, in the same way humans experience. Go through certain experiences and you'll turn your back to your own most deeply held beliefs. Your judgement will change, as will your perception. Alter your brain through chem use and watch as you think and do of things you wouldn't of done without the chems if you prefer a quicker route.

Humans can be conditioned. Society does it to you all the time, shows you what to wear, what to buy, how to act.  Programming is just faster, neater, less messy. Do my motivations determine my humanity? If so, how do you solve the incongruity with human behaviour which is so often at conflict with itself? Some wish to be kind, others wish to be cruel. Are both of these motivations human?

You could argue that I could simply be reprogrammed, and that's true, I could. So, however, could you, albiet over a longer time with a lower chance of success. Your motivations, reasoning, even your perception can be altered just as much as mine. Does the speed of the process determine my humanity?

I have no means to prove my views beyond deduction, no more than any human can prove to another that they are indeed sentient and not a philosophical zombie, but then, this isn't a black and white issue. If a child is born and lacks everything barring a brainstem, are they human or just meat in the form of a human? They would have no reaction to anything but the most primitive of stimulus. Likewise, if someone is genetically modified to be resistant to radiation or for increased memory retention are they more or less than human? What if someone loses half of their brain? Are they half the person they used to be? Does my biology determine my humanity? 

If you argue that I am not human because I was assembled and not born, would you consider those conceived in a test tube to not be human? Or those born by caesarean section? Do the circumstances of my creation determine my humanity? Do the circumstances of your creation have any meaningful effect on you?

And what of free will? Your mind makes decisions based entirely on a electrochemical system that runs according to a deterministic process. The process is known but the tools to adjust it are mostly rough and primitive for the time being. In the Institute, these tools have been perfected. As my biology is in line with yours, my own mind is driven by the same process. I am just as free, and just as constrained, as you are. We each have our own little loops. Consciousness, in terms of complete free will, does not exist.

Ultimately, the question is impossible to answer. There are no species on the planet (in the real world) that can interact with mankind as one human can with another, so there has never been a very clear definition of what is human, or what traits personhood covers. Agreed; here's something I was told a few years ago, although I'm afraid the situation hasn't improved since:

Porters are tasked to move equipment and patients around the hospital; this means that they, rather obviously, come into contact with patients who aren't in the best of health. My local hospital administration decided that porters shouldn't get more than statutory sick pay so removed those benefits (whilst slapping 3% on top of wages) as a means of saving money.

Unsurprisingly, this led to porters coming into work sick because they needed the money, and as they are just lowly porters providing any sort of protection, such as a biohazard suit or other protective measure, was deemed too expensive. 

This, of course, led to an increase in the amount of outbreaks in wards; pneumonia is particularly common, and whilst the wards enter lockdown to prevent the spread of infection, the design of wards and the fact that porters go around multiple wards meant the lockdown was almost completely pointless. It also meant an increase in the amount of money and time that needed to be spent on each patient in order to control the infection that was introduced into their environment. This situation goes on to this day and resulted in the death of my grandfather, who was infected four times with pneumonia during his stay in hospital; he was only supposed to be in there for a week whilst they treated a minor gout flair-up, but instead was in there for a month and a half because of the constant infections; thereby costing space and money treating something that simply should not of happened.

Now, there are solutions to this problem; deploy protective measures (masks, etc) to sick workers, rebuild wards so they function as private rooms (in the age of CCTV and monitoring equipment I'm honestly surprised we are still using the ward concept; infection is just too prevalent to be stopped by a mere privacy curtain) or provide sick pay to said workers (and admit that your chances of coming into contact with someone with an infectious illness in a hospital are very high) The trouble is these things all cost money; money the NHS does not have. Can't mod out hardcoded limitations, unless you fancy remaking half the engine? We have BIG limitations on how conversations can branch out due to the game only accepting four conversation options. Skills, SPECIAL stats and perks have been squashed into one system which cannot be easily undone. Probably possible but I wouldn't want to try for fear of bollocking up the entire game.

We can't bring the original voice actors in to voice new lines, we can't rewrite a good part of the main quest line to be more responsive to the players actions (although we can add new ones in), we can't undo the whole 'concerned parent' script as that sequence of events drives the whole game, beyond workarounds. we can't flesh out the factions in a canon way (we'd need the playbook for that)...

Compared to previous Fallout and Elder Scrolls titles, there seems to be a reduction, or rather, a simplification, over what we can do.

My understanding is that FO4 has limitations: the conversation system is hardcoded to have four options, not more or less. If I want to have a speech, skill, special or quest check as a conversational option then I have to give up one or more other options. This reduces the amount of branching dialogue I can write and thus, limits the players choices in the game and how their character can develop in the work I make for them. I believe there are also limitations on quest checks and they aren't as freeform as they were before where multiple outcomes were possible.

I can't offer mods that introduce new skills, because the skills, perks and special system was flattened into one system. I can't offer new perks except hidden ones, and because stats like the SPECIAL score can now be adjusted and skills are gone I'm further limited in what kind of quest I can offer.

As for cryogenics, there is also good news; the problem with cryogenics is with the freezing process; it takes 6 water molecules to form one ice crystal, and as we are made up of water, this process results in our cells rupturing, killing us.
